title: Boyle's Law (Gas Laws)
notes: **Statement of Boyle's Law:** For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume (V) is inversely proportional to the pressure (P). Mathematically: $V \propto \dfrac{1}{P}$ or $PV = k$, where k is a constant that depends on the amount of gas and the temperature.

**Derived equation for changing conditions:** If a gas changes from an initial state ($P_1$, $V_1$) to a final state ($P_2$, $V_2$) at constant temperature: $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$. This is the most commonly used form for solving numerical problems.

**Experimental basis:** Robert Boyle discovered this law in 1662 using a J-shaped glass tube sealed at one end. He trapped air in the closed end and added mercury to the open end, increasing the pressure. He observed that doubling the pressure halved the volume, and so on.

**Graphical representations:** (1) **P-V isotherm:** A curve (rectangular hyperbola) showing V decreasing as P increases — never touching either axis because neither volume nor pressure can be zero. (2) **V vs 1/P plot:** A straight line through the origin with slope = k, confirming direct proportionality between V and 1/P. (3) **PV vs P plot:** A horizontal straight line, showing PV is constant at a given temperature.

**Relationship between density and pressure:** Since density $d = m/V$ and mass is constant, substituting $V = m/d$ into $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$ gives $\dfrac{P_1}{d_1} = \dfrac{P_2}{d_2}$, or $P \propto d$. At constant temperature, increasing pressure increases density proportionally.

**Limitations — Real gases vs. ideal gases:** Boyle's law holds exactly only for **ideal gases** (no intermolecular forces, point particles). Real gases deviate at high pressure (molecular volume becomes significant) and low temperature (intermolecular attractions become significant). The deviation is measured by the **compressibility factor** $Z = \dfrac{PV}{nRT}$; for an ideal gas Z = 1, for real gases Z ≠ 1.
**Boyle's temperature ($T_B$):** The temperature at which a real gas obeys Boyle's law over a wide range of pressures. At $T_B$, the compressibility factor Z ≈ 1 for moderate pressures.

**Practical applications — Breathing:** During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, increasing thoracic volume. According to Boyle's law, increased volume causes decreased pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in. During exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes, volume decreases, pressure rises above atmospheric, and air flows out.

**Practical applications — Syringes and pipettes:** Pulling a syringe plunger increases volume inside the barrel, lowering pressure. Atmospheric pressure pushes liquid into the syringe. Similarly, using a pipette relies on creating a pressure difference by changing volume.

**Practical applications — Scuba diving:** As a diver descends, water pressure increases (~1 atm per 10 m depth). The air in the diver's lungs and equipment compresses. If a diver holds their breath while ascending, the expanding air (decreasing external pressure) can rupture lung tissue — a condition called **pulmonary barotrauma**. Divers must always breathe continuously and never hold their breath.

**Practical applications — High altitude:** At high altitudes, atmospheric pressure is lower. Weather balloons expand as they rise because the external pressure decreases. Commercial aircraft cabins are pressurised to simulate ~8,000 ft altitude pressure to prevent gas expansion in passengers' bodies.

**Practical applications — Deep-sea operations:** Pressure at ocean depths is enormous (1 atm per 10 m). Special diving suits and submersibles must withstand these pressures. Gas mixtures for deep-sea breathing (heliox) account for pressure effects on gas density and solubility.
confusion: **Constant temperature is critical:** Boyle's law applies ONLY when temperature and mass are held constant. If temperature changes, you must use the combined gas law ($\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$) instead.

**Inverse proportionality vs. direct proportionality:** Students sometimes reverse the relationship. Remember: as pressure INCREASES, volume DECREASES (inverse). This is the opposite of Charles's law where volume and temperature are directly proportional.

**Why the P-V curve never touches the axes:** Volume cannot be zero (the gas always occupies some space), and pressure cannot be zero (there is always some molecular motion). The hyperbola is asymptotic to both axes.

**Real gas deviation direction:** At high pressure, real gases have Z > 1 (less compressible than ideal) because molecular volume matters. At moderate pressure, many gases have Z < 1 (more compressible) because intermolecular attractions dominate.

**Confusing Boyle's law with the ideal gas law:** Boyle's law ($PV = k$) is a special case of the ideal gas law ($PV = nRT$) when n and T are constant. The ideal gas law is more general and applies when any variable changes.
practice: A gas occupies 2.5 L at a pressure of 101.3 kPa. What volume will it occupy at 202.6 kPa (temperature constant)? **Solution:** $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 \Rightarrow 101.3 \times 2.5 = 202.6 \times V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = \dfrac{253.25}{202.6} = 1.25$ L.

A syringe contains 50 mL of air at 1 atm. If the nozzle is blocked and the plunger is pushed to reduce the volume to 20 mL, what is the new pressure? **Solution:** $1 \times 50 = P_2 \times 20 \Rightarrow P_2 = 2.5$ atm.

A balloon has a volume of 3.0 L at sea level (101.3 kPa). What is its volume at an altitude where the pressure is 60.8 kPa? **Solution:** $101.3 \times 3.0 = 60.8 \times V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = \dfrac{303.9}{60.8} = 5.00$ L.

A gas at 25°C occupies 4.0 dm³ under a pressure of 760 mmHg. If the pressure is increased to 1520 mmHg at the same temperature, what is the new volume? **Solution:** $760 \times 4.0 = 1520 \times V_2 \Rightarrow V_2 = \dfrac{3040}{1520} = 2.0$ dm³.

The density of a gas is 1.5 g/L at 750 mmHg. What will its density be at 1500 mmHg at the same temperature? **Solution:** Since $P \propto d$ at constant T: $\dfrac{P_1}{d_1} = \dfrac{P_2}{d_2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{750}{1.5} = \dfrac{1500}{d_2} \Rightarrow d_2 = 3.0$ g/L.
universalFacts: Boyle's law was discovered independently by Robert Boyle (1662) and Edme Mariotte (1676); in France it is often called Mariotte's law.
The law is named after Robert Boyle, an Anglo-Irish natural philosopher who published 'New Experiments Physico-Mechanical, Touching the Spring of the Air' in 1660.
Boyle's law is one of the fundamental gas laws that, combined with Charles's law, Gay-Lussac's law, and Avogadro's law, gives the ideal gas equation: $PV = nRT$.
The P-V diagram (indicator diagram) is a powerful tool in thermodynamics for visualising gas behaviour and calculating work done during expansion or compression.
Boyle's law applies best to gases at low pressure (≤ 1 atm) and high temperature (well above the boiling point), where intermolecular forces are negligible.
